props.title: Fire at Sea

sections.content: **Fire at Sea** (2016) revolutionized refugee crisis documentaries by avoiding sensationalism. Director Gianfranco Rosi spent months on Lampedusa, capturing the Mediterranean migrant crisis through the dual perspectives of local islanders and desperate refugees. The film's power comes from its patient observation and striking juxtaposition - while 12-year-old Samuele practices his slingshot and struggles with lazy eye exercises, rescue operations pull drowning migrants from overcrowded boats. This masterful documentary influenced later migration films like Human Flow (2017) and **For Sama** (2019).

sections.content: The film marked a crucial shift in humanitarian crisis documentation. Unlike the sensationalized approach of **Born into Brothels** (2004) or the political messaging of **An Inconvenient Truth** (2006), Rosi lets raw reality speak through careful composition and editing. His camera lingers on faces, allowing audiences to connect with both islanders and refugees as humans rather than statistics. This influenced later works like Sea Sorrow (2017) and The Cave (2019).

Rosi's innovative structure weaves together seemingly disconnected narratives that build profound meaning. While local doctor Pietro Bartolo treats refugees, young Samuele battles anxiety and seasickness - a subtle parallel to the larger crisis. This technique of finding universal human experiences within specific stories became a template for films like Last Men in Aleppo (2017) and **The Missing Picture** (2013). sections.content: **Fire at Sea** (2016) transformed documentary aesthetics through its striking cinematography. Rosi's background in photography shows in every frame - from the metallic rescue blankets shimmering like modern-day Pietàs to the vast Mediterranean serving as both pathway and grave. This visual approach influenced later humanitarian documentaries like **Island of the Hungry Ghosts** (2018) and **Midnight Traveler** (2019), which similarly employ poetic imagery to explore migration themes.
